Choosing type for a design

A practical workflow for narrowing font choices and building a typography system.

Organized from Johnny’s reading notes, with clarifications and project ideas. Updated 21 October 2026.

Explore the Choosing Type roadmap

PurposeAudienceInspirationFont selectionSizingStyle guideResourcesIdeas

1. Identify the purpose

Begin with the information someone needs and the action they should be able to take. A portfolio visitor might need to understand your role in a project; a workshop attendee might need to find a time and location. These tasks give you criteria for evaluating type.

The medium is where the design will appear: a website, app, printed card, poster, or another format. Consider viewing distance, screen size, and how much text someone will read.

Choose the mood deliberately. In an illustrated greeting card, lettering can echo the illustration. On a landing page built around photography, quieter text can keep attention on the images. Typography works alongside imagery, color, spacing, layout, and interaction to communicate meaning.

Try it: Write the design’s purpose in one sentence, identify the medium, and choose two words describing the intended tone.

2. Identify the audience

Describe the readers and the conditions in which they will use the design. Consider reading experience, interests, language, cultural context, device, and accessibility needs. Age can provide context, but it cannot tell you an individual’s preferences or abilities.

For beginning readers, examine recognizable letter shapes and character distinctions. Your notes identify Sassoon Primary as a typeface to investigate. For readers who need larger text, evaluate size, contrast, spacing, and enlargement together. A font name alone cannot make a layout accessible.

Try it: Describe one reader, what they need to find, and a condition that could make reading difficult.

3. Gather and analyze inspiration

Collect a small set of references and describe the choices you can observe. Look at heading treatment, paragraph width, spacing, weight, and the relationship between text and imagery. Record what each choice contributes before borrowing it.

Study combinations as well as individual typefaces. Ask which face carries the main reading, which attracts attention, and how the roles remain distinct. Compare a version using one family with a version using two.

Try it: Collect three examples and write one specific reason each is useful. Use those observations to create a shortlist.

4. Choose fonts and their roles

Legibility concerns distinguishing characters. Readability concerns reading text comfortably in context. Test both using real titles, paragraphs, labels, and numbers from your project.

Some typefaces are designed for particular jobs, including display headings, extended reading, or compact interfaces. Look for the designer’s description and specimens, then test the candidate at the size where you plan to use it. Decorative detail can work in a short title while becoming tiring in a long paragraph.

Create hierarchy with a clear role for each style

A single family can provide headings and body text through changes in weight, size, and style. A second family can introduce useful contrast when it has a defined job. Check whether the combination makes the reading order clearer.

Treat the note about using no more than three fonts as a simplicity guideline. Count families separately from their weights and styles: one family with regular, italic, and bold does not require three unrelated families.

Try it: Compare three candidates with identical content. Assign heading and body roles, and explain what each choice contributes.

5. Determine sizes and spacing

Start with a comfortable body-text setting. A modular scale supplies related size options by repeatedly multiplying a base value by a ratio. For example, a 16px base and a 1.25 ratio produce 20px, 25px, and 31.25px.

Compare smaller steps with larger ones. A perfect fourth is about 1.333; the golden ratio is about 1.618. Larger ratios create larger jumps, which may not fit a dense interface. No ratio guarantees that a layout will look good.

Select the sizes your content needs, then adjust them by eye. You can round values when useful; whole pixels are not mandatory. Check line height, paragraph width, heading wraps, and the relationship between captions and body text on narrow and wide screens.

Try it: Test two ratios with the same content. Keep the sizes that establish a useful hierarchy and change any that cause awkward wrapping.

6. Create a typography style guide

Record the decisions so another person can apply them consistently. Include the family and fallback, role, size, weight, style, line height, letter spacing, color, and an example of use. Document responsive adjustments where they are needed.

Choose text colors within the wider palette while maintaining readable contrast. Include examples showing where expressive styles belong and where a simpler treatment is required. Shared text styles in design software and reusable CSS styles can carry these decisions into practice.

Review the guide against actual pages. Typography develops through experimentation: a documented decision can be revised when testing reveals a better option.

Try it: Document a title, paragraph, caption, and action label. Check whether someone else could reproduce them from your instructions.

Other references recorded in the notes

Creative Bloq’s free-font collection, Awwwards’ 2015 collection, InVision’s typography-resource collection, and the Behance Google Fonts Combinations volumes are recorded in the original article’s resource links. The Mailchimp typography pattern and Focus Labs example are also historical references there. Use that source to trace the original examples; their present availability has not been confirmed.

For broader exploration, browse Behance and Dribbble. Sketch appears in the notes as an example of software with reusable text styles.

Font identification: distinguish inspecting a live website’s CSS from identifying lettering in an image. The notes use “WhatTheFont”; the original reading links a browser extension under that label. Browser developer tools can inspect a live page’s font declarations without relying on that historical extension link.

Ideas to explore

A guided font preference assessment

Replace an overwhelming catalogue with a sequence of smaller decisions. Answers could build a project-specific preference profile and rank a shortlist of fonts and possible pairings.

Possible formats include numbered agreement scales, scales between opposing descriptions, forced choices, and repeated comparisons of two visual examples. Candidate assessment areas are purpose and medium, reading needs, desired mood, visual preferences, and text roles.

The proposed database would identify Google Fonts and system-font candidates and associate them with descriptive attributes. Required language coverage, available styles, and platform availability could filter candidates before preference scores rank them. System-font availability would need to be checked by platform.

Keep project requirements and aesthetic preferences visible in the results. Explain why each candidate fits and show it with real content. The metrics, weighting, font attributes, and pairing rules are still to be designed; this is a proposed feature.

A typography comparison gallery

Collect website examples in a grid and isolate their typography. Compare an original with a controlled font substitution to see how the page’s character changes. Record what changed in hierarchy, spacing, wrapping, and the relationship with imagery.

Questions for further study

What other elements communicate with users?
Explore imagery, color, layout, spacing, symbols, and motion alongside text.
How is a typeface’s intended use documented?
Look for designer descriptions and specimens, then test the stated role.
When does decorative type help?
Compare its contribution in a short heading with its effect in sustained reading.
When is one family enough?
Compare one family with multiple weights against a heading-and-body pairing.
